title: How to Broker Peace in Ukraine
gist: Waldman and Charap argue that eighteen months of U.S.-led Russia-Ukraine diplomacy have failed because the process itself is poorly designed — unilateral, fragmented across separate bilateral texts, and lacking agreed rules or agenda — and that adopting mediation best practices (multilateral contact groups, interest-based bargaining, confidential channels, an interim cease-fire framework) offers the more promising path, even as Putin faces his weakest battlefield momentum since the 2022 invasion.

insights.claim: Russian forces advanced by less than half a square mile per day in June 2026, a reduction of more than 90 percent from their rate of gain in June 2025, while Ukraine's long-range drone strikes are disrupting Russia's energy sector, state revenues, and daily life in major Russian cities ahead of September's Duma elections.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Quantifies why Putin may be under his most significant pressure since the 2022 invasion, a signal for the credibility of near-term negotiation windows and for Russian energy-sector disruption risk.

themes.theme: Design flaws in the current process

insights.claim: Unlike successful multiparty mediation efforts — the 1995 Bosnia contact group of France, Germany, Italy, Russia, and the UK, or the 2016 Colombia-FARC talks backed by Chile, Cuba, Norway, and Venezuela — Washington has largely gone it alone on Russia-Ukraine, with European allies, Gulf partners, and Turkey involved only at the margins.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Identifies structural under-involvement of European stakeholders as a specific, correctable process flaw rather than an intractable feature of the conflict.
insights.quote: In Ukraine, by contrast, Washington has largely gone it alone.
insights.locator: In Ukraine, by contrast, Washington has largely gone it alone

insights.claim: The authors recommend Washington establish a formal European contact group modeled on the Bosnian precedent, giving key European governments defined roles rather than observer status, citing British national security adviser Jonathan Powell's Good Friday Agreement negotiating experience as untapped expertise.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable proposal — watch for any formal European contact-group structure being announced as a signal the process is being redesigned along more credible lines.

insights.claim: By some accounts, nearly half of all peace agreements fail within five years, and a Russia-Ukraine settlement faces even longer odds given incompatible territorial claims, the legacy of the failed Minsk agreements, and the broader NATO-Russia rivalry.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Sets a base-rate expectation for durability even if a settlement is reached, relevant for pricing in renewed-conflict risk after any eventual agreement.

insights.claim: The Russia-Ukraine talks have never brought all four key parties — Kyiv, Moscow, Washington, and key European states — to a single table around one text; instead, four separate bilateral draft texts exist (US-Ukraine, Europe-Ukraine, Russia-Ukraine, and Russia-US), risking that terms acceptable in one channel undermine the whole process.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: A concrete structural vulnerability: incompatible parallel texts could produce a deal that unravels when parties compare notes — worth watching if reported terms diverge across negotiating channels.
insights.quote: different combinations of the four have discussed separate draft texts: one between Ukraine and the United States, another between Europe and Ukraine, a third between Russia and Ukraine, and a fourth between Russia and the United States.

insights.claim: No mutually agreed negotiating agenda appears to exist for the Russia-Ukraine talks, unlike Colombia's 2012 General Agreement, which laid out guidelines, an agenda, and ground rules that provided structure for the eventual 2016 peace accord.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Absence of a shared agenda is a diagnosable, fixable gap — its emergence (or continued absence) is a leading indicator of whether talks are maturing.

insights.claim: Every diplomatic effort to end the Russia-Ukraine war over the past year and a half has played out via a media circus, in contrast to the discreet prisoner-of-war exchange channel, which has remained almost entirely out of view and produced consistent, meaningful results.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Suggests public, high-profile negotiating tracks are less likely to succeed than quiet, low-visibility channels — a heuristic for judging which reported diplomatic 'breakthroughs' deserve credibility.

insights.claim: The U.S. has repeatedly presented finished, take-it-or-leave-it proposals — including the 28-point plan leaked in November 2025 and subsequent pressure on Kyiv to cede the Donbas — rather than helping the parties develop their own solutions, an approach mediation research shows produces compliance only as long as external pressure is sustained.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Implies that U.S.-imposed settlement terms, even if formally signed, carry higher breakdown risk once U.S. attention or leverage wanes.
insights.quote: The 28-point plan leaked in November 2025 and the subsequent attempts to get Kyiv to cede control of the Donbas exemplify the approach.

insights.claim: Citing Henry Kissinger's Sinai mediation, where Egypt's core interest was sovereignty and national pride while Israel's was security, enabling a security-for-sovereignty bargain, the authors argue mediators should target Russia's and Ukraine's underlying interests over the Donbas rather than their stated territorial positions.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Provides a specific historical template for a possible Donbas compromise structure — worth watching for signs negotiators shift from territorial haggling to interest-based framing.
insights.quote: Egypt’s core interest was sovereignty and national pride while Israel’s was security.

insights.claim: The authors recommend widening the negotiating agenda so territory, security guarantees, and sanctions relief are discussed together rather than in separate channels, since a broader basket creates more room for cross-issue tradeoffs and strengthens incentives to comply with any eventual deal.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: A specific process reform that, if adopted, would signal negotiators are shifting toward a more durable settlement structure.
insights.locator: Putting everything on the table creates more room

insights.claim: Because Ukraine and its Western backers want an immediate cease-fire before talks while Moscow wants a political settlement before any cease-fire, the authors propose an interim framework agreement with limited political commitments sufficient to secure a cease-fire, with a fuller settlement process to follow.
insights.speaker: Matt Waldman
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete bridging mechanism to watch for as the most likely near-term deliverable, short of a full peace deal, that could reduce fighting-related market and energy disruption.
